title: Fowl brought forth by the waters, or formed from the ground? The Hebrew of Genesis 1:20 does not say the waters bring them forth
summary: The KJV of Genesis 1:20 and Brenton’s Greek have the waters bring forth fowl, while Genesis 2:19 forms the fowl from the ground. The Hebrew of 1:20 has the waters swarm with living creatures and the fowl fly, as a separate clause.
text: KJV Genesis 1:20: “Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth” KJV Genesis 1:21: “which the waters brought forth abundantly” KJV Genesis 2:19: “out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air”. Hebrew (WLC) 1:20: יִשְׁרְצ֣וּ הַמַּ֔יִם שֶׁ֖רֶץ נֶ֣פֶשׁ חַיָּ֑ה [the waters swarm with a swarm of living creatures]; וְעֹוף֙ יְעֹופֵ֣ף עַל־הָאָ֔רֶץ [and fowl fly above the earth]. Hebrew (WLC) 2:19: מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ וְאֵת֙ כָּל־עֹ֣וף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם [out of the ground, every beast of the field and every fowl of the heavens]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:20: ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [let the waters bring forth creeping things having life, and flying birds above the earth]. Brenton Greek 2:19: ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πάντα τὰ θηρία τοῦ ἀγροῦ, καὶ πάντα τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [God formed further, out of the earth, all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the heaven]. NETS (New English Translation of the Septuagint) 1:20: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things among living creatures and birds”, with birds flying on the earth; NETS 2:19 has God furthermore form from the earth all the animals of the field and all the birds of the sky. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN01.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN02.htm and https://ccat.sas.upenn.edu/nets/edition/01-gen-nets.pdf. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: Read in the KJV, the waters bring forth the moving creature and the fowl in chapter 1, while chapter 2 forms the fowl from the ground. Brenton’s Greek of 1:20 has one verb, “let the waters bring forth”, governing both the creeping creatures and the flying birds, so the Greek reads as the KJV does. The NETS English translation of the Septuagint confirms that reading of the Greek: its 1:20 has the waters bring forth creeping things among living creatures and birds. The Hebrew has a verb for the waters (they swarm) whose object is the swarm of living creatures, and then a separate clause in which the fowl themselves fly. On the Hebrew wording, chapter 1 does not say what the fowl came from, and 2:19 says they were formed from the ground. The conflict therefore exists in the KJV and the Greek, and is not clearly present in the Hebrew.
scope: This is a demonstrated difference in clause structure, not a difference between synonymous English words. It does not show that the Hebrew has no tension with chapter 2: it says the fowl fly above the earth, and 1:22 has the fowl multiply “in the earth”, and some readers take the fowl to be among the creatures the waters produce. Genesis 1:24 has the earth bring forth the land animals, which is consistent with 2:19 for the beasts. The Hebrew is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text, and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament); NETS is an English translation of the Septuagint and is cited only to show how the Greek is read. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees. Presence of this record is not a claim of exhaustive review.

title: Male and female created together, or the woman made after the animals?
summary: Genesis 1:27 reports man created, male and female. Genesis 2 has the man formed first, the animals brought to him, and a woman made later from his rib.
text: KJV Genesis 1:27: “male and female created he them” KJV Genesis 2:18: “It is not good that the man should be alone” KJV Genesis 2:19: “brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them” KJV Genesis 2:22: “made he a woman”. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: In chapter 1 the creation of man as male and female is a single act. In chapter 2 the woman is made only after the man has been alone and the animals have been brought to him. The two can be read as a summary followed by a detailed account, or as two accounts with a different order. The text does not say which.
scope: This record concerns where the woman appears in the two sequences. It does not repeat the animals-and-man order covered by beasts-and-fowl-formed-before-man-or-after, which cites Genesis 2:19; it places a different verse pair on a related question. Interpretations that Genesis 1 summarizes Genesis 2 are preserved as possible readings. No Hebrew or Greek comparison was made, so no H or G tag is proposed.

scope: This record places the Abraham appearances on a question the Jacob record (jacob-saw-god-face-to-face-or-no-man-hath-seen-god) already asks, under the standing ruling that a new verse may have its own record when the existing study does not cite it. title: Cain a fugitive and vagabond in the earth, yet he builds a city?
summary: Cain is told he will be a fugitive and a vagabond. He then dwells in Nod and builds a city.
text: KJV Genesis 4:12: “a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth” KJV Genesis 4:16: “dwelt in the land of Nod” KJV Genesis 4:17: “he builded a city”. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: A wanderer without a settled home and a man who dwells in a land and founds a city are different conditions. The narrative moves from the curse to the settlement within six verses without comment. The curse is tied to tilling the ground, so it may describe the loss of farming rather than permanent travel.
scope: The text does not say how long Cain wandered before Nod, or whether Nod is a place or a condition. Readings that the curse was partly lifted, that the city came later, or that the words describe loss of farmland are reasonable and are preserved. The record does not address who else lived in the earth. No Hebrew or Greek comparison was made, so no H or G tag is proposed.

title: God repents, or is not a man that he should repent?
summary: Genesis 6:6 says it repented the Lord that he had made man. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say God is not a man that he should repent. 1 Samuel 15:11 has the Lord say “It repenteth me” in the same chapter.
text: KJV Genesis 6:6: “it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth” KJV Numbers 23:19: “neither the son of man, that he should repent” KJV 1 Samuel 15:11: “It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king” KJV 1 Samuel 15:29: “he is not a man, that he should repent”. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: The KJV uses “repent” of God both as an act and as something God does not do. In 1 Samuel 15 the two statements are 18 verses apart. The usual reconciliations are that one sense is regret and the other is a change of purpose, or that the denials are about fickleness.
scope: The same English word in the KJV does not by itself show the same word in the original. A shared root does not settle the sense, and no Hebrew comparison was made here, so no H tag is proposed. Per the standing ruling on synonymous English words, this is held at the KJV level until the Hebrew is examined. Reconciling readings are preserved.

title: Noah entered the ark before the flood, or on the day it began?
summary: Genesis 7:7 has Noah go into the ark because of the waters. Genesis 7:10 says the waters came after seven days. Genesis 7:11-13 dates the flood to a day and says Noah entered in the selfsame day.
text: KJV Genesis 7:7: “Noah went in, and his sons” KJV Genesis 7:10: “after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth” KJV Genesis 7:11: “the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up” KJV Genesis 7:13: “In the selfsame day entered Noah”. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: Genesis 7:7-10 puts the entry seven days before the waters came. Genesis 7:13 puts it on the day the fountains broke up, which Genesis 7:11 gives as the day the flood began. Both are in one narrative.
scope: Genesis 7:7 may be read as a summary that is expanded in 7:13, and “selfsame day” can mark the day the whole embarkation was complete. These readings are preserved. The record is a comparison of the surviving narrative, not confirmation of a flood. No Hebrew or Greek comparison was made, so no H or G tag is proposed.

title: Four hundred years of affliction, or four hundred and thirty years in Egypt?
summary: Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 give four hundred years. Exodus 12:40-41 gives four hundred and thirty years for the sojourning in Egypt. Galatians 3:17 gives four hundred and thirty years from the covenant to the law.
text: KJV Genesis 15:13: “they shall afflict them four hundred years” KJV Exodus 12:40: “was four hundred and thirty years” KJV Galatians 3:17: “the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after” KJV Acts 7:6: “entreat them evil four hundred years”. DRAFT: proposed for Codex verification and owner acceptance; not yet integrated.
reasoning: The numbers differ by thirty years, and the starting points differ. Genesis and Acts speak of a stay in a land not theirs and of affliction. Exodus speaks of the time the children of Israel dwelt in Egypt. Galatians counts from the covenant to the law.
scope: Four hundred can be a round number, and the affliction may have begun after the sojourning did. Other ancient texts of Exodus 12:40 are reported to read differently; that was not examined here. The count of years is a comparison of the numbers given, not a dating of the exodus. No Hebrew or Greek comparison was made, so no H or G tag is proposed.
